1:
The word that ends Baasha's house arrives through a young man whose father was still prophesying. John Gill (reformed) identifies Jehu as the son of that Hanani who had reproved Asa, so a prophet's son and himself young, since he is found years afterward reproving Jehoshaphat and writing the annals of that reign. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reads the genealogy the same way and dates it from the same later appearances (2 Chron. 19:2; 20:34). Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) grants that nothing else is known of the man, and adds the detail that costs: Hanani was imprisoned for the faithful discharge of that same ministry to Asa (2 Chron. 16:7-10). Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) sets father and son side by side — the father sent to Judah, the son on the longer and more dangerous errand north, juniores ad labores — and thinks prophecy so entailed worthy of the more honour.

Henry takes the warning itself as the mercy in it: God threatens that he may not strike, so that if Baasha reforms the ruin is prevented, and if he does not, the destruction will appear plainly as justice rather than accident. Ellicott notices how closely the oracle tracks Ahijah's against Jeroboam, and draws from the parallel that Baasha had a probation which he neglected. On being lifted out of the dust Gill reads a very low estate and a mean family; Henry presses the theology of it, that a man who seemed to make himself by treachery was all the while serving a counsel not his own (1 Sam. 2:8), and that God's owning the advancement is no patronage of the means. Clarke puts the same guard in stronger terms: the making of a prince here is providential permission, for it is impossible that God should make a rebel and a murderer king over his people.

The sentence is Jeroboam's sentence over again. Gill marks that the posterity goes by death with no branch remaining, and that the dogs and the fowls deny them burial exactly as was threatened and executed on the house before them. Henry's comment is that those who resemble others in sin may expect to resemble them in plagues, and that the pattern will run on past Baasha to the house of Jehu itself (Hos. 1:4). Then the reprieve. Baasha dies in his bed and is buried in Tirzah with honour; Gill notes the death was natural and not violent. Henry will not let that pass as escape: the greatest delinquent neither sees nor feels the threatened stroke, his iniquity is laid up for his children (Job 21:19), and the judgment specified falls on bodies after death — which he takes as a tacit intimation of punishments beyond what death can reach.

Verse 7 then says it all again, and the witnesses divide over why. Gill reports Abarbinel's answer, that the first threatening was for making Israel sin and this one for Baasha's own works. Ellicott hears the historian's own voice, a note added chiefly for the sake of the last clause, which shows that the act, though foretold, was not thereby justified. Clarke suspects dislocation and would place the verse between v.4 and v.5; he also canvasses four candidates for the man Baasha killed — the Vulgate's Jehu the prophet, or Baasha, or Jeroboam, or Nadab, the last carrying Jarchi and some good critics with it. Henry reads it of Jeroboam's son and house, and draws the edge of the chapter from it: had Baasha struck with an eye to God's glory he would have been accepted as a minister of justice, but he was its tool and his own lusts' servant, which is why those who denounce or execute judgment must do it from a good principle or make themselves obnoxious by it.
8:
Elah's two years are not two full years: John Gill (reformed) counts him dead within Asa's twenty-seventh, and observes that he lasted exactly as long on the throne as Nadab the son of Jeroboam did — the parallel the chapter keeps insisting on. The man who ends him held a divided command. Gill, following the Targum, makes Zimri one of two captains over the war-chariots, and Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) supposes a colleague not named here who commanded the other half of the cavalry. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) hears in the description of the king's debauchery an emphasis of half-contemptuous condemnation — it was public, it was in the house of a mere officer of his household, and it went on while the war at Gibbethon was still being fought; whereas Zimri, pointedly called his servant, seems to have been the high officer left in charge of the palace and the king's person while the mass of the army was in the field.

Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) extend the suspicion to the host: Arza the prefect of the palace was no doubt a party to the conspiracy, and had probably arranged the drinking bout in his own house for the purpose of carrying it out. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) is harder on the victim than on the plot, measuring Elah against the king he replaced in the pattern — Nadab fell in the field of action besieging the same city, where Elah should have been commanding in chief and was not, having loved his ease and safety above his honour, his duty and the public good. From that he takes the plain warning: death comes easily on men in that condition, who are the more easily overcome by an enemy and the less able to help themselves, and it comes terribly, finding them in the act of sin and unfitted for any act of devotion, so that the day arrives unawares (Luke 21:34).

What follows is extermination, and the witnesses measure its reach. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the coarse idiom of total destruction as covering males only, explained by the clause that follows it — neither the blood-relations who might have avenged his death nor his friends. Henry notes that this went further than Baasha's own purge of Jeroboam's line, which left avengers where Zimri left none, and that the traitor succeeded to a people who tamely submitted; he holds by cruelty what he got by treason, and the justice that overtook him so quickly became a proverb long afterward (2 Kings 9:31) — the same passage Ellicott cites for the proverbial force of Zimri's name. Clarke adds a rabbinic severity, that when such a sentence is determined not only the man's house is destroyed but the five neighbouring houses with it, that his memory may perish from the earth; Gill traces the reach to everyone connected with Baasha even in friendship.

The reason given is idolatry father and son. Gill reads the double naming as proof that Elah trod in Baasha's steps and was cut off for it, and Clarke draws the same conclusion about why judgment was permitted to fall on the family at all. Keil and Delitzsch render the grammar closely — the destruction is on account of all the sins, committed through their nothingnesses, by which the golden calves are meant. Ellicott takes the word for those nothingnesses further: it covers not only the idols of Dan and Bethel but the worse abominations that grew up under their cover, and he observes that Scripture's scorn for idolatry as gross folly, faith wasted on unrealities, runs at least as strong as its condemnation of idolatry as outrage against God's law (Isa. 44:9-20; Ps. 115:4-8).
15:
Seven days is all the text allows Zimri, and John Gill (reformed) reads it flatly: he reigned until the army came up, took the palace and destroyed him. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) fills in the campaign — Israel was besieging a Philistine city when word came that Zimri had killed the king, whereupon the troops made their own general king, raised the siege, and marched on Tirzah, where Zimri, finding his case desperate, chose to burn rather than be taken. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) draws the constitutional moral from how little the elevation needed explaining: it shows how entirely the kingdom of Israel had become the prize of the sword, and by a curious coincidence Baasha's own dynasty had been founded in the camp before that same city. He adds that the conspiracy must have been hastily made, with no adequate support behind it, since the capital falls at once. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) hears Solomon behind it — for the transgression of a land many are its princes (Prov. 28:2) — and notes that the army never avenged Nadab on Baasha, whose house had ruled more gently, but would avenge an idle and intemperate king on his murderer.

Gill measures the march at thirty-six miles on Bunting's reckoning and finds Tirzah lightly fortified; Henry calls it beautiful but unwalled, and reads the self-burning as two motives at once, that his rival should never enjoy the palace and that his own body should not be ignominiously used alive or dead. Ellicott works on the word the English renders palace: its derivation gives the high place or citadel, and though some make it the harem — with which the Septuagint's odd word for a cave or lurking-place might agree — he judges the term itself does not suggest it. The act, he adds, has many parallels in Eastern history and suggests that something in the assassination of Elah was held especially treasonable.

Why a king of seven days should be charged with walking in the way of Jeroboam divides the witnesses three ways. Ellicott offers the historian's own sense of a curse lying on the whole kingdom through its idolatry, which Zimri never repudiated — or else, he allows, the conspiracy had dressed itself as zeal for Jehu's prophecy and dropped the pretence once the deed was done; for otherwise there was no time for such walking. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) take the clause grammatically instead, attaching it to the verb of dying in the previous verse: he died, that is, as punishment for his sins. Henry supposes the plainer thing, that Zimri in fact lived some while past the seven days of his proclamation and in that space showed his inclination and upheld the calves.

Then the kingdom splits. Gill sees a contested succession and very probably a battle in which Tibni's party was worsted. Clarke confesses the cause unknown and divides the sides by institution — the people for Tibni, the army for Omri, and the army prevailed. Keil and Delitzsch take the people of Israel here for the fighting people, so that the throne was settled by the host; and Ellicott makes Tibni himself a military chief, possibly Zimri's own colleague under Omri's command, noting that the Septuagint gives him a brother Joram who fell with him. On the arithmetic the terse verse conceals they agree: Henry dates Omri's election to Asa's twenty-seventh year and his unrivalled reign to the thirty-first, and Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both put the struggle at about four years. Henry closes with a question he borrows from Sir Walter Raleigh — why, through all these revolutions, Israel never thought of returning to the house of David — and answers with him that dread of a heavier yoke kept them attached to kings of their own.
23:
Twelve years will not fit between Asa's thirty-first and Ahab's accession, and the witnesses meet the gap differently. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) says outright that there must be a mistake in the number, then accepts Jarchi's harmony out of Sedar Olam: the division began in Asa's twenty-seventh year and lasted five, Omri holding only a share, and Tibni dying he held the whole for seven more. John Gill (reformed) reaches the same total without impeaching the text, counting the twelve from the twenty-seventh year when Elah was killed, and putting the division at four years by the Jewish chronology though Jarchi says five. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) reckon likewise from the rebellion against Zimri, leaving the sole government seven years and a few months, and explain the six years at Tirzah as four of civil war plus two after Tibni's death. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) also puts the struggle at four years, and sees the accession opening nearly half a century of settled government.

Ellicott is alone in reading Omri's policy as a whole. The king had to buy peace from Syria by acknowledging its sovereignty and ceding cities; he then allied himself with the royal house of Tyre, for strength against Syria and for a revival of Solomon's commerce; and he built a new capital in a strong position, the phrase about the might he showed marking him for a soldier. Like Jeroboam and Baasha he had the opportunity to restore his people's spiritual strength, and threw it away. Clarke accounts for the move more locally: Tirzah had suffered badly in the civil broils and been burnt over Zimri's head, so a fresh seat was wanted.

What the hill cost is given three ways — two talents reckoned by Gill at seven hundred and fifty pounds on Brerewood's valuation, by Clarke and Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) at a little over seven hundred, and by Keil and Delitzsch in thalers. The name divides them further. Clarke would render the clause from the Hebrew — he bought the hill of Shomeron from Shomer and called it Shomeron, Little Shomer — and Keil and Delitzsch likewise derive it from the former owner. Ellicott grants the owner but will not stop there: the Hebrew name means a watch-tower, and he thinks a double derivation likely, from the position as much as the man. He calls the site a soldier's choice — an isolated hill with precipitous sides rising in a basin of the hills of Ephraim, near the maritime plain and commanding the sea — vindicated by the sieges it withstood and by the Assyrian inscriptions that name it the house of Omri. Clarke carries it through Ben-hadad, Shalmaneser's three years and the Asmoneans to Herod's restoration and the name Sebaste. Henry's interest is the wandering — Shechem, Tirzah, Samaria, while Judah's kings held to Jerusalem, for those who cleave to the Lord fix and those who leave him ever wander — and he alone conjectures that Shemer may have sold cheaper on condition the city bear his name.

The verdict converges. Gill reads the evil as done openly, in defiance. Clarke grades it: an idolater in principle, in practice and in teaching, and worse than all before him in making statutes for idolatry and obliging his subjects by law to commit it. Henry draws that line exactly — Jeroboam caused Israel to sin by allurement, Omri by compulsion — and Ellicott notes that Micah's phrase for the statutes of Omri stands in parallel with the works of Ahab's house as a symbol of hardened apostasy (Mic. 6:16), suggesting Baal was anticipated before Ahab formally brought him in. Henry allows the might its due and no more: many a bad man has been a stout man, has built cities and left his name in history, and has no name in the book of life.
29:
The chapter's superlatives have been climbing; here they change kind. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) put the difference precisely: the kings before Ahab had only perpetuated Jeroboam's sin, the worship of Jehovah under the image of an ox, and Ahab was not satisfied with that — the Hebrew turns on a question, was it too little?, so that because those sins were too small a thing he took Jezebel, the following verbs being pictorial, marking a new turn rather than a continuation. John Gill (reformed) makes the same distinction plainly: the earlier kings at least pretended to worship God in the calves, whereas Ahab worshipped other gods beside him. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) frames it by the commandments — it was nothing to him to break the second by image-worship, so he would set aside the first as well — warning that making light of lesser sins makes way for greater.

The marriage is where Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) locates the head and chief of the offending: the idolatrous daughter of an idolatrous king, who practised it openly, rewarded its partisans, and put the prophets and priests of God to death. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) traces the fanaticism to the father. Ethbaal, whom he and Keil and Delitzsch both identify from Menander in Josephus, was a priest of Astarte who took the throne of Tyre by assassinating Pheles, and is styled here not king of Tyre, as Hiram was, but king of the Zidonians — an older name whose revived spirit may account for the devotion to Baal visible in Jezebel and in Athaliah after her. Ellicott reads the match as the fatal turning-point for a man physically brave and perhaps able to govern but morally weak, and finds the history returning to the supremacy of his wife's harder nature; Keil and Delitzsch add that her name probably means untouched. Henry thinks Ahab knew what she would bring and married her for it, and judges that this one wife debauched Israel further than all the wives of Solomon (2 Kings 9:22).

On the god himself the witnesses are closer than they look. Ellicott describes the Zidonian Baal as the productive principle in nature, with Astarte as the receptive, and insists the name is a title meaning lord, marked as such by the article that nearly always precedes it — which is why it attaches to the supreme god of several mythologies and survives in Baal-peor, Baal-berith and a string of place-names. He lists its forms: sometimes the Sun, sometimes the planet Jupiter, sometimes a half-humanised Tyrian Hercules. Henry canvasses the same three, and adds a motive of his own — that Ahab had grown weary of the golden calves and, like men sick of their own idols, must have variety. Gill explains the building practically, that a temple at Samaria spared the court the journey to Tyre or Zidon; Henry sees rivalry in the siting, Baal's house in the royal city because God's stood in the royal city of the other kingdom.

The grove divides them. Gill allows a plantation with an idol in it but prefers to read the word as Astarte herself, an image of the Zidonian goddess; Clarke takes it the same way, citing a Syriac version that calls it an idol and an Arabic that calls it a tall tree, which he reads as an image of Priapus, keeper of gardens; Keil and Delitzsch call it the Asherah belonging to the temple of Baal; Ellicott says it represented the Phoenician Astarte and was enforced by Jezebel with a high hand. Henry stands alone for the trees, arguing from the verb — the text does not say he planted but that he made a grove, something that answered the purpose of concealing and so countenancing the impurities of the worship, since he that doeth evil hateth the light.
34:
The chapter closes on a private man, and the witnesses agree why. John Gill (reformed) notes that the work was done by Ahab's leave, which is why a builder's enterprise is reckoned among a king's wicked actions; Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) read the refortifying of a cursed site as a measure of how far ungodliness had advanced, and its outcome as proof that the Lord will not let his servants' word be transgressed. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) presses the imitation, a subject copying his king's presumption, and marks that the man came from Bethel, where one of the calves stood. Gill allows either ignorance of Joshua's adjuration or open contempt of it, with the added motive that the work would please the king and queen; Henry has him jesting with the curse as a bugbear, or reckoning its force worn out by the five hundred years since it was pronounced (Josh. 6:26), and compares him to Achan for turning to his own use what was devoted to God's honour.

Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) will not let the terms of the curse pass as plain. He sets out three readings of laying the foundation in the firstborn and setting the gates up in the youngest. The first takes the sons to have died, the eldest at the founding and the rest in succession until the family was extinct as the doors were ready to hang. The second makes the words a proverb for protracted labour: the builder spends on it the whole span in which he fathers children, so his last son is born before the walls will take their gates. The third has him sacrifice the firstborn to consecrate the work and the youngest in gratitude at its completion, a reading he finds countenanced by the Chaldee, which has Hiel slay both. Clarke then weighs them. Only the Chaldee implies the children died at all; the Vulgate, Septuagint, Syriac and Arabic do not, and the manuscripts give no help. He adds two objections — why should innocent children suffer for their father's presumption, and would a man who had lost his firstborn at the founding have gone on at the risk of the rest? — then declines to say which opinion is right, or whether any is.

Henry takes the first reading without hesitation, and makes it the verse's point: the man built for his children and God wrote him childless, the eldest dying when he began and the youngest when he finished, with all the rest, it is supposed, between — and he went on building after the curse had begun to execute itself. Clarke also records that the Syriac names Ahab himself as the builder, the Arabic calling the city a house of idols. Of its present state he reports a curse still seeming to rest there — not blotted off the map but reduced to some thirty wretched cottages and a dilapidated castle, with no ruin left to show what it had been.

Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reads the same act as evidence of prosperity as well as impiety, and corrects a common assumption: the site had not been wholly deserted before this. What was new was its importance, kept down to Herod's time. He accounts for that by the ground — well watered, beautiful and fruitful, the city of palm trees, and militarily valuable, commanding the pass from the Jordan valley up to Ai and Bethel. The territorial anomaly he presses hardest. Jericho had been assigned to Benjamin and should properly have belonged to Judah, so a Bethelite rebuilding it under Ahab's patronage is for Ellicott a sign of how half-dependent the southern kingdom had become. Keil and Delitzsch note the same allotment and resolve it more simply, that the city had passed into Israel's hands when the ten tribes fell away from the house of David.
